b: Data Mesh and Data Products need a Self-Service Platform

One of the core principles of Data Mesh is the need for a self-service
data platform. To achieve decentralized ownership, domain teams must be
empowered to build, deploy, and manage their own data products without
friction or cognitive overload. A self-service platform provides the
necessary abstractions, automation, and tools to make this autonomy
possible.

A well-designed platform should incorporate key data mesh concepts like
data contracts and data products. Data contracts ensure a controlled and
stable handover of data between teams. Data products act as the unit of
reusability for productized data and can be connected to each other to
form the network or 'mesh' in which decentralized ownership can be
assigned.

Figure 1: A high-level overview
of a self-service data platform empowering the creation and lifecycle
of data products across domains.

To build a complete data product, we need various technologies such as
compute to run data transformations, data storage, data ingestion tools,
data catalogs, query engines, quality tools, and more. When we examine
these technologies, we often find a significant gap because they typically
lack the necessary abstractions for concepts like data contracts or data
products.

This “platform gap” arises because a single data product requires a
combination of these technologies to function as an integrated whole.
Thus, no single underlying technology can cover the whole data product
either. The absence of built-in abstractions often leads to confusion
about what a data product is and how it manifests within the technology
stack. This complexity can make it difficult for teams to use the
available technologies directly, hindering the adoption of data mesh
principles.

Figure 2: The Platform Gap, illustrating a
disconnect between high-level Data Mesh concepts and the underlying data
technologies.

The obvious solution to the platform gap is to engineer a platform that
sits on top of the existing data technologies. This new layer should raise
the level of abstraction, reduce cognitive load for developers, and
provide a user experience centered around data contracts and data
products. The goal is to automate and integrate the experience, creating a
truly self-service platform.

However, building such a platform is not without its challenges.
Platform teams often struggle to articulate their progress, prioritize
their work, and demonstrate the value of their investments. This is where
a structured approach, guided by a maturity model, provides clear
guidance.

Figure 3: Platform engineering
bridging the platform gap by creating a new layer of abstraction on top of
existing data technologies.
The Platform Navigator: CNCF Maturity Model

The platform engineering community, through the Cloud Native Computing
Foundation (CNCF), has published the Platform Engineering Maturity
Model. This model provides a framework for assessing and advancing
platform capabilities, making it an excellent navigator for a data mesh
journey.

The CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model is defined by several
maturity levels and a set of aspects that evolve as the platform
matures.
Operational: A more standardized and centrally managed platform.
Scalable: A self-service platform that encourages adoption.

Optimizing: A platform that is continuously improving and deeply
integrated into the development workflow.

The aspects of the platform that are assessed at each level
include:
Investment: How staffing and funds are allocated to the platform.
Adoption: How and why users discover and use the platform.

Interfaces: How users interact with and consume platform
capabilities.

Operations: How platform capabilities are planned, prioritized,
developed, and maintained.

Measurement: How feedback is gathered and incorporated to improve the
platform.

Figure 4: The CNCF Platform Engineering
Maturity Model, showing the four levels Provisional, Operational,
Scalable, Optimizing and the five aspects (Investment, Adoption,
Interfaces, Operations, Measurement).
How to Use the Maturity Model

Figure 5: The three-step process for using
the maturity model: 1. Know your current platform maturity, 2. Focus on
high friction aspects, 3. Iterate.
Using the maturity model is a straightforward process:

Know your current state: The first step is to map your
current platform situation against the different aspects and maturity
levels. For example, we might have a dedicated team for platform
investment (Level 2), but operations and measurement might still be
ad-hoc (Level 1).

Figure 6: Mapping the current state of a
platform on the maturity model grid, and indicating planned improvements
on aspects with high friction.

Focus on a specific aspect: Once we have a clear picture of
the current state, we can focus on a specific aspect to improve. For
instance, if we want to ensure we are building the right features, we
might decide to invest in a platform product team and start collecting
insights on the biggest pain points for our users.

Iterate: The final step is to apply our improvements and
continuously adapt.

As we iterate, we must remember to balance the different aspects of the
maturity model against each other. Some aspects, such as Investment and
Adoption, heavily revolve around people, policies, and processes, while
others, like Interfaces and Operations, are more focused on technology. By
using the maturity model grid as our compass, we can consciously guide
our next steps. For example, we might realize we need to balance our
investments by focusing on self-service solutions and automated central
enablement (technology) only after we have established a dedicated
product team and collected insights (people, policies, and processes). This
balance prevents us from over-investing in one area while leaving others
behind, and the model helps us clearly communicate these strategic
decisions to stakeholders.
The Four Levels of Platform Maturity for Data Products and Data Mesh
Level 1: Provisional Platform - The “No Platform” Platform

A provisional platform for data products and data mesh is characterized
by an ad-hoc and chaotic approach to technology and provisioning. To
illustrate this, let's use a bit of domain storytelling.

Figure 7: Domain storytelling
for a provisional platform, showing developers making ad-hoc requests to
different engineers for various components, leading to a chaotic mix of
technologies.

Consider a first data product developer who sets out to create a new
data product. Lacking a central self-service platform, they must navigate
the organization through personal networks. They start by talking to a
DevOps engineer [1] to request a source control repository, and that
engineer creates a Git repository [2] on the Git platform. Next, the
developer needs a build and deployment automation pipeline, so they talk
to a second DevOps engineer [3], who creates a CI pipeline [4] on the CI
system. For data storage, the developer talks to a cloud engineer [5], who
creates an S3 bucket [6] on AWS Cloud. With the basic infrastructure in
place, the developer sets up their own data processing tools: they create
an Iceberg database [7] on an Iceberg catalog and query engine, and create
a Spark job [8] running on a Spark cluster. By manually assembling these
disparate pieces, they produce something that resembles a data
product.

Sometime later, a second data product developer is tasked with building
another data product. Having no platform documentation or self-service
interface to guide them, they talk to the first developer [9] to ask how
to get started. The first developer refers them to the DevOps engineer who
helped them earlier. The second developer then talks to that same DevOps
engineer [10], who creates another Git repository [11] on the Git
platform. Next, the developer talks to the second DevOps engineer [12],
who creates another CI pipeline [13] on the CI system.

When choosing their analytical technology stack, however, the second
developer takes an entirely different direction. Rather than using Iceberg
and Spark, they create a dataset [14] on Google BigQuery, run a dbt model
[15] on dbt Cloud for transformations, and create a view [16] on a data
virtualization tool to serve the data.

This scenario highlights the core failure modes of a provisional
platform. Data technology is requested and provisioned entirely ad-hoc,
with human bottlenecks at every step where developers must “know someone
who knows someone that knows how to do something” to make progress. There
is no explicit concept of a data product or data contract. There are only
isolated, manually stitched pieces of technical infrastructure. The result
is too high a cognitive load, deep technological fragmentation and
complexity, and increasing shadow IT across the organization.
Level 2: Operational Platform - The “Fragmented” Platform Experience

At the operational level, there is an effort to standardize technology
and track requests centrally. However, the experience for data product
developers remains fragmented and complex.

To introduce order into the chaos, organizations typically establish
dedicated infrastructure teams (e.g. a DevOps Team, a Cloud Team, and a
Data Platform Team). Requests are then channeled through a centralized
ticketing system like Jira.

Continuing the story, the data product developer now has to request
every component through formal tickets:

The developer creates a Git Repository Ticket [1] in the ticketing
system. Sometime later, the DevOps Team reads the ticket [2] and
provisions a Git repository [3] on the Git platform. The developer then
creates a CI Pipeline Ticket [4], which the DevOps Team reads [5] to
provision a CI pipeline [6] on the CI System. For storage, the developer
creates an S3 Bucket Ticket [7], which the Cloud Team reads [8] to
provision an S3 bucket [9] on AWS Cloud. Turning to data infrastructure,
the developer creates an Iceberg Database Ticket [10], which the Data
Platform Team reads [11] to provision an Iceberg database [12] on the
Iceberg Catalog & Query Engine. Finally, the developer creates a Spark Job
Ticket [13], which the Data Platform Team reads [14] to provision a Spark
job [15] on the Spark Cluster.

While this introduces central visibility and standardizes the
technology catalog, it replaces personal tapping-on-shoulders with queues
and handoffs. Waiting for multiple teams to fulfill tickets takes
significant time. More critically, once all these individual components
are provisioned, the developer is still left entirely alone to glue them
together into a functioning data product. Frustrated by the delays and
integration friction, developers are often tempted to bypass the platform
altogether, managing [16] their own shadow IT solution (“My Data
Platform”) to deliver results faster.

At the operational level, automation can be introduced through typical
Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) scripts (e.g. Terraform) to speed up the
provisioning of individual components. This will avoid ticketing systems
and human bottlenecks.

Figure 9: Domain
storytelling for an operational platform, showing developers using limited
Infrastructure-as-Code automation, but still having to manually glue the
components together.

In this alternative setup, each
specialized team provides reusable scripts that developers can execute
independently. The data product developer executes the
createGitRepository script [1], which automatically
provisions a Git repository [2] on Git. The developer then executes the
createCIPipeline script [3], which provisions a CI pipeline
[4] on the CI System. For cloud storage, the developer executes the
createS3Bucket script [5], provisioning an S3 bucket [6] on
AWS Cloud. For data assets, the developer executes the
createIcebergDatabase script [7], provisioning an Iceberg
database [8] on the Iceberg Catalog & Query Engine, and executes the
createSparkJob script [9], provisioning a Spark job [10] on
the Spark Cluster.

While this script-based automation eliminates ticketing delays, the
developer is still left with the complex task of gluing everything
together to create a data product. The cognitive load remains high, and
there is a knowledge bottleneck, as developers need to know how to compose
data products from these different components (e.g. configure and
integrate networking, security roles, storage, pipelines, secrets, etc).
When errors occur, developers run into knowledge gaps and still need [11]
direct human help from the DevOps Team, Cloud Team, and Data Platform
Team.

Ultimately, this operational approach leads to a lack of uniformity:
organizations end up with “Frankenstein” data products that look similar
on the surface because they use the same underlying technologies, but are
architecturally inconsistent under the hood. Exhausted by the complexity
of stitching everything together, developers frequently retreat to shadow
IT, continuing to manage [12] their own local platforms (“My Data
Platform”).
Level 3: Scalable Platform - Platform as a Product

A scalable data mesh platform represents a major shift in the
developer experience. The interface changes completely, moving from
individual technologies to a higher-level, data product-centric
abstraction.

Figure 10: Domain storytelling for a
scalable platform, showing a developer interacting with a self-service
portal that handles the provisioning and integration of data
products.

In this scenario, the organization establishes a
dedicated Data Product & Data Mesh Platform Team that treats the
platform as a product. Rather than handling tickets or providing
disconnected scripts, this team provides a self-service developer
experience consisting of a Data Product Developer Portal and an underlying
Data Mesh Platform Backend.

The domain
story is much simpler. In summary, a data product developer just clicks
'Create Data Product', and the platform wires the technology and
infrastructure together as a Data Product. In the domain storytelling
diagram above, the developer creates a Data Product [1] on the Data
Product Developer Portal by defining its architectural specification
such as input and output ports, data transformation code setup, and data
contracts for the structure and guarantees on the data. The portal
captures this intent and instructs the Data Mesh Platform Backend to do
the provisioning and integration of components.

From this single
declaration, the Data Mesh Platform Backend automatically orchestrates
the underlying technical resources across all infrastructure domains: it
provisions a Git repository [2] on Git, provisions a CI pipeline [3] on
the CI System, and provisions an S3 bucket [4] on AWS Cloud. In the data
infrastructure domain, the backend provisions an Iceberg database [5] on
the Iceberg Catalog & Query Engine, and provisions a Spark job [6] on
the Spark Cluster.

Instead of just spinning up isolated components, the backend
automatically wires and glues them together into a cohesive,
standardized data product.

This integrated self-service tooling transforms the developer
experience. The cognitive load on developers drops significantly because
they interact with the abstraction of a data product rather than
wrestling with underlying technologies. It removes the knowledge
bottleneck: developers no longer need to be infrastructure plumbing
experts who know how to hand-stitch security permissions, pipelines, and
storage configurations. Furthermore, because the platform backend
enforces architectural standards, every data product exhibits more
technical uniformity, which prevents “Frankenstein” data products. When
every data product adheres to the same standardized architectural
structure, the platform can enable automated governance by injecting
automated policy checks, audit logging, access controls, and data quality
verification across all data products. By making data product creation
easy, straightforward and frictionless, it encourages voluntary
adoption, naturally discouraging shadow IT.

By removing the knowledge bottleneck, the platform empowers data
product developers with more autonomy, which is crucial for scaling a
data mesh and data product management practice across multiple domain
teams.
Level 4: Optimizing Platform - Platform as an Ecosystem

At the optimizing level, the platform becomes deeply integrated
into the daily developer workflow. Rather than requiring developers to
switch contexts and go to a platform portal, the platform comes
directly to the developer's working environment and context.

Figure 11: Domain storytelling for
an optimizing platform, showing the platform integrated into the
developer's local environment IDE/CLI and an ecosystem of teams
contributing to the platform.

This shift is achieved in the developer's local context by making
the tools they live in every day (e.g. IDE or CLI) “data product
aware.” The domain story illustrates how this streamlines the entire
data product lifecycle:

The data product developer creates [1] a local Data Product
directly from their day-to-day workspace. Through an IDE Plugin or a
dedicated CLI, the developer can create, develop, deploy, and monitor
the data products from within their familiar environment without
disruptive context switching.

The local tools communicate with the platform and create [2] the
Data Product on the centralized Data Mesh Platform Backend (which is
maintained by the Data Mesh Platform Team).

From there, the
Data Mesh Platform Backend automatically provisions and integrates the
necessary technologies needed for the data product. A Git Repository
is provisioned on Git [3] and a CI Pipeline on the CI System [4]. In
AWS Cloud, an S3 Bucket is created [5] to store data in the data
product. Structure is given to the data using an Iceberg Database [6]
on an Iceberg Catalog & Query Engine. And finally, the data product
comes alive when a Spark Job is running in the Spark Cluster [7].

Just as in Level 3, the platform backend automatically handles all
the wiring and integration so the provisioned resources are glued
together to function as a single, cohesive data product.

Another defining dimension of the optimizing level is the emergence
of a federated platform ecosystem. The central platform team no longer
acts as a bottleneck for new capabilities. Instead, other teams across
the organization can contribute directly to the platform backend:

An engineer from a Domain Team can contribute a domain-specific extension,
such as Platform Capability X (e.g. specialized data product templates), making
it available to the entire organization [8].

An engineer from a Specialized Team (such as security, compliance, or data
governance) can contribute platform capabilities, such as Platform Capability Y
(e.g. automated PII masking, fine-grained access policies, or audit logging)
[9].

An optimizing platform for data products and data mesh minimizes
context switching for developers, manages the entire data product
lifecycle, and enables an ecosystem of contributors. Managing the
entire data product lifecycle empowers the organization to execute
migrations of data products when underlying technologies evolve (e.g.
upgrading an Iceberg or Spark version, breaking changes in data
contract formats, etc), without requiring every team to rewrite their
data products. Actively tracking which platform capabilities and which
data products are actually consumed allows teams to prune unused data
products and decommission obsolete platform features, continually
refining and evolving the platform to meet organizational needs.
Minimal Maturity Level for Data Mesh Success

Given these different levels of maturity, what is the minimum
level required for a successful data mesh implementation?

Figure 12: Minimal maturity levels for
Data Mesh success, highlighting the Scalable level as the minimum
requirement.

The provisional level is essentially chaos. There is no real
platform, and domain teams are left waiting for resources or
building their own solutions. It's impossible to build a
decentralized, interoperable mesh with disconnected and unmanaged
tools.

The operational level, while more organized, still presents
significant challenges. The high cognitive load and fragmented developer
experience mean that teams are still responsible for gluing the pieces
together themselves. This is a common trap for organizations that focus on
automating the provisioning of individual technologies without addressing
the overall developer experience. The complexity and friction often lead
to low adoption rates and a continuation of shadow IT. After having
invested only in standardizing and automating individual technologies,
many data mesh journeys get stuck at this level, because it is too complex
and costly for domain teams to participate.

This brings us to the scalable platform for data products and data
mesh. This is the minimal level for success. At this stage, the platform
team transitions from an IT helpdesk to a product team focused on
developer experience and bridging the platform gap. By allowing developers
to interact with the abstraction of a data product, the platform removes
the complexity of the underlying technologies, encouraging voluntary
adoption and enabling the decentralized ownership that is at the heart of
data mesh.

There is an interesting relationship between platform maturity and user
adoption. Up to and including the operational level, leadership has to
push the platform by mandating its use through policies and architectural
review boards. In large organizations, engineers will find their way
around painful platform tools and find the path of least resistance
through shadow IT. So the platform struggles with adoption. The platform
is simply too complex and difficult to use.

It is only when a platform reaches the scalable maturity level that we
begin to see a significant increase in adoption because using the platform
is just easier than doing it yourself (i.e. “Intrinsic Pull”). Even then,
adoption doesn't skyrocket overnight. The platform team needs to
evangelize the platform and educate users to drive adoption. However, the
scalable level is the point where voluntary adoption becomes possible,
which is a prerequisite for a successful data mesh that needs to be
adopted by many domain teams.

Figure 13: The Platform Adoption Curve, showing low
adoption for provisional and operational levels, with adoption taking off
at the scalable level.

The Platform Engineering Maturity Model serves as a compass for the
self-service platform in a data mesh journey. It allows to make targeted
investments to improve platform maturity and drive adoption. By assessing the
current maturity level, we can identify the aspects causing the most
friction and invest in improving them. This iterative approach allows to
pull up the overall maturity of the platform and ensure that
all aspects are taken care of.

As illustrated in the sequence above, a journey rarely moves
all five aspects forward in lockstep:

Step 1: A potential starting point is where all five aspects
sit at the provisional level: ad-hoc technology, fragmented requests, and no
dedicated platform team.

Step 2: A common trap is where teams push into technology only
and build self-service interfaces and automate operations (Level 3).
Adoption still lags behind at Level 2 because nobody is spreading the word
on how easy to use the platform is. There is also the risk of building
capabilities nobody needs as measurement for feedback remains ad-hoc at Level 1.
Organizational enablement and feedback gathering need to get priority urgently.

Step 3: Using the model as a compass, the
organization makes a course correction. Rather than adding more technical
features, the team directs its next investment cycle into the lagging aspects.
They transition to a platform-as-a-product mindset, collect actionable usage
insights, and drive voluntary adoption through evangelizing the platform,
embedding with domain teams, and refining the developer experience. This
brings all five aspects to the scalable level, reaching the minimum for data
mesh success.

Step 4: With a foundation in
place, subsequent investment cycles pull the platform forward into Level 4 by
integrating capabilities into local IDEs and CLIs, enabling contributions from
domain and specialized teams, and leveraging measurements and feedback for
continuous optimization.

This is only one example of a scenario where investments are bringing the
self-service data product platform to an increasing level of maturity.
Every organizational context might be different and focus on different aspects first,
which is completely fine. We can use the maturity model to detect what is lagging behind and keep
balancing people, processes, and technology.

Building a self-service platform for data products and data mesh requires
balancing different aspects. On a technical level the platform should
lower cognitive load significantly and be as easy-to-use as possible. At the
same time it is not a purely technical project, because we want people to
adopt the platform without pushing them to do so.

By using the Platform Engineering Maturity Model as our navigator, we can
assess where our platform stands today, uncover the aspects causing the most
friction, plan small steps for improvement, and iterate on this. The model
allows us to explain our progress, what priorities we want to invest in,
and the value of our investments to stakeholders to get buy-in and
funding.

If you are wondering where to begin on your own journey, start small: bring
this maturity model to your next platform or architecture discussion. Map
where your capabilities sit today, identify the single area creating the
most friction for your domain teams, and focus your next investment cycle
right there.

The end goal is to bridge the platform gap and move from a fragmented and
mandated toolchain to a data product and user-centric self-service platform
that truly empowers teams to succeed with data mesh, data products and data
contracts.
